frames.narration: A shop has 6 modules and 6 teams. Version one is a big ball monolith: 1 deployable, 1 shared database, and callers that reach into each other's internals.
Product asks to rename a column in the Orders table. Every module reads that table, so all 6 modules are edited and all 6 teams must release together, in 1 deploy.

The team makes it a modular monolith: still 1 deployable, but each module owns its tables and is reached only through an interface. The same rename edits 1 module. Still all 6 teams share the release, so the release train is the remaining cost.

Now 6 microservices, each with its own data. The rename edits 1 service and releases alone: 1 deploy, 1 team. A checkout now makes 5 network calls, and if Payments fails only 1 of 6 modules stops working.

A shortcut keeps the 6 services but shares one database and one library. The rename edits 6 services and needs 6 deploys with 6 teams in lockstep. This is the distributed monolith: 5 network calls per checkout and a failure in Payments stops 6 of 6 modules.

Another team goes the other way: each module becomes 3 services (api, logic, store). A framework upgrade needs 18 deploys, and a checkout makes 17 network calls, which is 34 ms at an assumed 2 ms per call.

Over four changes (a price rule, an Orders contract field, a column rename, a framework upgrade) the deploys are: big ball 4, modular monolith 4, microservices 12, distributed monolith 18, nanoservices 27. Team-releases (teams that had to ship, summed over the changes): 24, 24, 12, 18 and 12.

A monolith has few deploys but a shared release and shared fate. Services buy independent releases and contained failures, and charge network calls, contracts and operations. Cut where teams really need to move alone, and own the data on each side of the cut.
